claims.text: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment currently exhibit inadequate resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
A thin, adherent chromium-based diffusion coating can be produced on a boride surface using diffusion treatment or sputtering.
The chromium-based coating will promote in situ formation of an aluminide/oxide layer during exposure to molten aluminum.
The in situ aluminide/oxide layer will be stable and adherent under hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
The passivation layer will form at the interface between the chromium-modified region and molten aluminum.
The passivation layer will act as a barrier that prevents direct contact between molten aluminum and the underlying boride substrate.
The chromium-associated passivation layer will reduce wetting of the boride surface by molten aluminum.
Reduced wetting and interfacial contact will suppress reactive attack of molten aluminum on the boride phase.
A chromium-based surface film can improve corrosion resistance relative to an uncoated surface.
The coating will reduce the molten-aluminum corrosion rate by at least 50% relative to untreated boride components.
Approximately 660–750°C is the typical operating-temperature range for hot-dip aluminum plating.
The proposed improvement should persist over exposure durations representative of industrial hot-dip aluminum processing.
Temperatures significantly above the normal range or prolonged exposure may degrade the coating or passivation layer and diminish protection.
Cyclic thermal stresses may compromise the long-term adhesion stability of the diffusion coating.
The kinetics of passivation-layer formation are not yet established and require experimental calibration.
Weight loss per unit area and corrosion penetration depth can be used as quantitative response variables in the proposed comparison.
Exposure at 700°C for 100 hours is industrially relevant.
